27.0.0.en: After the trial of Christ in the house of Caiaphas the high priest, they brought Him up to the council of the Sanhedrin (ch. 5:20-21) in one of the porticos of the Temple. This was at dawn, and they judged Him to death. For in the Jewish system, to pass a sentence of death on anyone there had to be more than one session, and likewise no one could be sentenced to death except in the daytime.

27.0.1.en: This was the third trial of Christ, and the last religious trial. In it they decided to kill Christ, and they arranged the case that they would present to Pilate so that he would kill Him. They had agreed on the following: (1) To ask Pilate to approve their decision to put Him to death.

27.0.2.en: (2) If he did not approve, they would accuse Christ of claiming to be the King of the Jews, and thus of being a rebel against Caesar and an agitator of the people against the authority, and they would claim that He forbids the payment of tribute, in order to stir up the civil authority against Him so that it would agree to kill Him.

27.0.3.en: (3) To accuse Jesus of blasphemy, since He declared that He is the Son of God.

27.0.4.en: Pilate's response to them was as follows:

27.0.5.en: (1) He did not approve their decision to kill Christ.

27.0.6.en: (2) He examined their second accusation and found Him innocent, and did not approve their decision to kill Him.

27.0.7.en: (3) He took no interest in the matter of blasphemy, because it concerned their own law and is not punished by Roman law. Nothing was left for them but to insist on the second accusation, namely His claim to be the King of the Jews. They put Pilate in a difficult position, and he, fearing to be considered a supporter of Christ against Caesar, was compelled to agree to what they said, and he ordered His crucifixion.

27.1.0.en: Pilate was governor of Judea on behalf of the Roman authority. He was cruel and shed the blood of many, and he held office for ten years. The Jews complained of him often to Caesar, but he was weak in holding to the truth and was concerned to keep his position.

27.1.1.en: Do not try to look for accusations against those who annoy you in order to stir up others against them, using your mind in an evil way. By doing so you bring God's anger upon yourself, your heart is troubled, and you lose the love of those around you, even if they support you in what you say or do, because they sense your hostile thoughts.

27.2.0.en: “He was condemned”: the Jews judged that He should be put to death.

27.2.1.en: “What is that to us?”: Your words do not concern us; we have obtained what we wanted, which was the arrest of Christ. “See thou to that”: You are responsible for your own guilt, so act as you wish, away from us; we will not help you in anything. When Judas learned that the Jews had condemned Christ to death, his conscience pricked him and he felt the horror of his betrayal. Indeed, the silver became a weight that pained his heart and reminded him of his sin. He went in the morning to the Temple and found that they had taken Christ to Pilate, but a few of the priests were still there. So he threw the silver down before them in order to be rid of what was pricking his conscience, and he confessed that Christ was innocent and that he was a traitor for having betrayed Him to them. But sadly, it was remorse without hope. It was not repentance, because repentance is faith in God and hope in life with Him, not mere remorse. As for the priests and elders, they tried to shed their sin by refusing the silver, and told Judas to bear his own guilt, since they were not responsible.

27.2.2.en: How could this be, when they were about to carry out His killing a little later?! It is the deception with which man deceives himself so that he does not repent.

27.3.0.en: When the priests refused to take the silver from him, he threw it before them to be rid of it, thinking that this would free him from the feeling of guilt, and he left the Temple and even the whole city. But his conscience continued to prick and rebuke him, and he could not bear it; he went and hanged himself. Most likely he hung himself with a rope on the mountain, and he was strangled, then his weight fell on the rope, so it came loose from the mountain and he fell, and he burst open and his bowels gushed out, as the Apostle Peter mentioned in the Book of Acts (Acts 1:18).

27.4.0.en: The chief priests could not put the silver into the treasury chests in the Temple because it was the price of a man's blood, and they considered the gifts placed in the treasury to be holy. Although they knew all this, they did not repent, and they continued in their evil until they crucified Christ.

27.5.0.en: “They took counsel”: the members of the council of the Sanhedrin, after they had delivered Christ to be crucified.

27.5.1.en: “The potter's field”: a field called by this name, perhaps because its soil used to be taken to make pottery, and so it was called that. It is not suitable for farming, so its price was cheap, and it could only be built upon.

27.5.2.en: “Strangers”: Jews who were strangers to Jerusalem, if they died there, and who were poor and had no place in which to be buried.

27.5.3.en: “The field of blood”: because they bought it with the price of a man's blood, who is Christ.

27.5.4.en: “Unto this day”: the time when Matthew the Evangelist wrote his Gospel.

27.5.5.en: The priests found a solution, which was to buy something with this silver for a charitable purpose. So they bought the potter's field and set it apart as a burial place for strangers who had no place to be buried, and that field was called the field of blood, confirming the horror of their sin. Their hiding behind a charitable deed could not erase their sin.

27.6.0.en: By this evil of theirs they fulfilled what was prophesied by the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 18:2, 6) about the potter's field, and by the prophet Zechariah (Zech 11:13) about the price of this field, which was thirty pieces of silver.

27.6.1.en: Thus we find that all the details of Christ's sufferings for all of humanity were prophesied in the Old Testament so that the Jews might believe, but sadly they hardened their hearts and crucified Him.

27.6.2.en: Beware, do not harden your heart and reject the rebuke of others, the words of the Holy Bible and spiritual sermons, but regard them as messages from God that alert you and bring you back to His love, so that you repent of your sins.

27.7.0.en: The trial of Christ began before the Roman authority, represented by the governor Pilate, and it was the fourth trial of Christ. Pilate asked Him: Art Thou the King of the Jews? And He answered in the affirmative, so that perhaps Pilate would reconsider and not fall into the sin of handing Him over to the Jews, not because He was drawing back from accomplishing redemption, but so that Pilate would be without excuse and would realize that he stood before a King, and so would not rush to pass any evil sentence on Him.

27.7.1.en: In His conversation with Pilate, as John mentioned (Jn 18:36-37), Christ made clear that His kingdom is spiritual and not earthly, and so the Jews' claim against Christ, by which they tried to stir up Pilate to condemn Him, failed. When Pilate learned that He meant a spiritual kingdom, he judged Him innocent when he said that he found no fault in Him (Lk 23:4, 14; Jn 18:38).

27.8.0.en: The chief priests and elders of the Jews tried to bring accusations against Christ before the governor Pilate, concerning His stirring up the people, as Luke the Evangelist mentions (Lk 23:5). Jesus did not defend Himself, because He knew the Jews' insistence on pinning false charges on Him, and He also knew the weakness of Pilate, who, though he knew His innocence, tried to please the Jews out of fear of them, and tried to catch a word from Christ with which to condemn Him.

27.8.1.en: The governor marveled at His silence and asked Him why He did not answer their claims so as to prove His innocence. But He remained silent. This increased the governor's amazement all the more, because those accused in such circumstances defend themselves so as not to be sentenced to death. Christ did not need to defend Himself, but wanted to accomplish our salvation by His death on the Cross.

27.8.2.en: Thus the innocence of Christ appeared once more before Pilate. He had sent Him to Herod when he learned that He was a Galilean and also learned that Herod, the ruler of Galilee, was visiting Jerusalem. When the latter tried Him and found no fault in Him (Lk 23:15), which was the fifth trial, he sent Him back to Pilate to try Him in the sixth and final trial.

27.8.3.en: Thus the innocence of Christ appeared three times, twice before Pilate and once before Herod. But because of his weakness, Pilate could not release Him (see the number of the religious and civil trials, ch. 26:66). If others have kept silent about your mistakes, do not persist in them, but examine yourself in order to repent.

27.9.0.en: Pilate found himself before an innocent, peaceable man, in whom he found no fault worthy of death. And because Pilate was weak in character, he could not declare His innocence. So he thought of a way to deliver Him from death, but without making enemies of the Jews, because he was seeking his position and the people's goodwill toward him. It was the custom to release to the Jews one of the prisoners at the feast of Passover, to show his leniency and kindness toward the Jews. So he asked them whether he should release to them Jesus, or an imprisoned criminal called Barabbas, who was notorious for crime and well known to the people. He knew that Jesus was innocent, and that the chief priests and elders envied Him because He drew the crowds by His love, His teachings and His miracles.

27.9.1.en: “Were gathered together”: he means the common people and not the chief priests, because he thought that, since Christ had done good to them, they would ask for His release.

27.10.0.en: God warned Pilate once more, so that he would not sin against Christ and sentence Him to death, for his wife sent to him warning him not to do anything harmful to Christ, because she had seen a dream on the night of His trial confirming the righteousness of Christ, and how much suffering He was enduring without guilt.

27.10.1.en: The Holy Bible does not mention the details of the dream, but it is a testimony to the righteousness of Christ from a pagan woman, at the time when the Jews were condemning Him to death and His disciples and all who loved Him were fleeing.

27.10.2.en: “This day”: that is, in the night of the day, which is counted as part of it. This means that the dream was a divine revelation, because the Jews had not yet brought Christ to Pilate when she dreamed her dream at night.

27.11.0.en: With malice and envy, the priests and elders of the Jews stirred up all the people gathered before Pilate to ask for the release of Barabbas, who was known for his crime, and for the killing of Jesus. So they tried to praise Barabbas and make excuses for him in his crime. As for Christ, they tried to pin charges on Him in order to convince the people to ask for Barabbas to be released.

27.12.0.en: After Pilate left the Jews to think it over, he asked them whom they wanted released to them, Jesus or Barabbas, and they all said: Barabbas. He asked them what he should do with Jesus, and they said: Let Him be crucified. Perhaps the leaders were the ones who began demanding His crucifixion, and the crowds followed them.

27.12.1.en: Crucifixion was the means of putting criminals to death among the Romans, and it was what would have fallen on Barabbas, but the Jews asked that it be carried out on Christ.

27.13.0.en: Pilate asked them again, weakly, what evil He had done, perhaps so that they would draw back from their decision, as if the decision belonged to the people and not to him! It is the height of cowardice ... So the Jews cried out all the more, demanding the crucifixion of Christ.

27.13.1.en: Thus God gives them more than one opportunity, that perhaps they might repent, but they insisted on their evil in killing the Righteous One.

27.13.2.en: We note here that two warnings had already preceded for them: the first from Christ Himself, that He comes to judge the whole world (Jn 5:22), and He would judge them for their evil in killing Him (ch. 26:24). The second warning was on the lips of Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Him, when he declared His innocence (v. 4). And the third warning was when Pilate washed his hands before them, declaring the innocence of Christ, as will be explained in (v. 24).

27.13.3.en: God warns you many times to turn back from your sins, so do not stop your ears and persist in your evil.

27.14.0.en: “A tumult was made”: that is, an uproar in the city (Jerusalem), for which Caesar would blame him, and which would be a cause of his removal for failing to control and keep order in the city.

27.14.1.en: “He washed his hands”: a custom known in ancient times to indicate that a person is not responsible for what happens before him (Deut 21:6).

27.14.2.en: “See ye to it”: that is, you are responsible for the judgment and His killing.

27.14.3.en: Pilate declared that Christ was righteous and innocent, and he washed his hands before all the people to declare his innocence of the crime of killing Jesus. But this by no means relieves him of responsibility for killing Him, because it was in his power to protect Him and not hand Him over to the Jews. But because of his weakness, he feared their shouting, and cared more for his position as governor than for the truth.

27.15.0.en: The gathered Jews declared their responsibility for the killing of Christ, in order to encourage Pilate to order His crucifixion, and they said: “His blood be on us, and on our children.” For when someone accuses a person of a charge and his innocence later appears, the punishment falls on the accuser, as happened with those who accused Daniel (Dan 6:24). And the crime of crucifying Christ still rests on every Jew who has not believed in Him.

27.15.1.en: And in submission and weakness, Pilate ordered Christ to be scourged and handed over to the Jews so that they might crucify Him.

27.15.2.en: “Scourged”: whoever was sentenced by the Romans to crucifixion was scourged first. The Roman scourging was cruel, for they struck with leather thongs at the ends of which were sharp pieces of metal, which wounded severely the one they scourged.

27.15.3.en: Hold fast to the truth whatever it costs you, because the truth is God, and your cowardice in declaring it is a rejection of God. Do not leave an innocent person to be wronged when it is in your hand to defend him, and do not seek your own interest and forget the interest of another who is wronged.

27.16.s.en: (5) The mocking and torture of Christ

27.16.0.en: After they had scourged Him and put His clothes on Him, they brought Him into the governor's residence, and the soldiers of the Roman cohort, about 600 soldiers, gathered against Him, because it seems that the Jews had warned Pilate about the followers of Jesus, who might start a revolt and seize Him. Therefore he gathered all this number of soldiers against Him.

27.17.0.en: They stripped Him a second time, for they had taken off His clothes first when they scourged Him, and they had no pity on His body, bloodied and torn by the lashes. Then they put a scarlet robe on Him, which seems to have been an old robe from the royal garments stored in the governor's residence. This scarlet color, also called purple, that is, dark red, signifies the blood and the redemption that He would accomplish for the salvation of humanity.

27.18.0.en: To carry their mockery further, instead of placing a crown of gold and jewels, they plaited a crown of thorns and pressed it onto His head, and it resembled a full covering for the head (a cap). How painful it was!! And instead of holding a scepter (a rod of gold or ivory that kings hold in their hands), they put a reed (a small staff of cane wood) in His right hand, then they bowed before Him mockingly, saying: “Hail, King of the Jews.” The Righteous One bore our sins, and endured what we ought to have endured. For the sinner strikes himself with the lashes of lust that tear him, and thinks that by fulfilling them he is a king, and puts on royal garments in pride, and the crowns of honor of which he boasts are perishable material things and the cursed earth that brings forth thorns and thistles, so that nothing covers his head but anxiety and pain. And having lost his authority over himself, he becomes like a reed (a weak plant like cane) shaken by the wind, that is, he is swept along with the current of the evil world. And, to carry his self-deception further, he rejoices in words of flattery and the false respect offered to him by those who profit from him.

27.19.0.en: They continued to mock Him and despise Him, and they spat upon Him, and took the reed and struck Him on His head, bloodied by the thorns.

27.19.1.en: This was the third mocking of Christ. The first was by the servants of the Temple in the house of Caiaphas (ch. 26:67, 68), and the second by Herod and his soldiers, which Luke the Evangelist mentions to us (Lk 23:11).

27.20.0.en: After they had mocked Him in every way, they gave His clothes back to Him and led Him away to be crucified. This was at the third hour, for the trial before the council of the Jews was early on Friday. As for the three civil trials, they began early and extended to the third hour, when Pilate delivered Him to the soldiers to crucify Him. If you are exposed to mockery or contempt, do not be troubled, because your God has endured every insult for your sake, and He is the Righteous and Holy One. So endure for His sake, and be confident that He will support you, and will even reveal your righteousness and reward you in heaven, and grant you inner peace on earth in these afflictions.

27.21.0.en: Christ carried the Cross and went with it from the governor's residence to outside Jerusalem. His body was exhausted and full of wounds and bruises, and His weakened body could not continue the journey under the weight of the Cross. This confirms the humanity of Christ, for He took a real body that was worn out by the many lashes. So that the soldiers leading Him would not be delayed, they seized a man called Simon, a farmer returning from his field, and compelled him to carry the Cross without payment and walk behind Christ so that they might quickly reach the completion of His crucifixion. This man was a Jew from Cyrene in North Africa, that is, in present-day Libya, and it seems that signs of pity for Christ appeared on him, so the soldiers took advantage of that and made him carry the Cross; and they did not carry it themselves because it was a sign of shame.

27.21.1.en: Simon signifies the Church of the New Testament, that is, the believers who carry the Cross behind Christ, as a sign of love for Him, by leaving every sin and enduring sufferings for His sake.

27.22.0.en: They came to a place outside Jerusalem called Golgotha, a Hebrew word meaning the skull. There is an ancient tradition that Adam was buried there, and for this reason the place was given this name. And behold, the Second Adam, Christ, is crucified in it to redeem Adam and all his children.

27.22.1.en: He was crucified outside Jerusalem, just as they used to bring out some sacrifices and slaughter them outside the camp where they dwelt; for Christ bore all the shame and disgrace, and was rejected by all.

27.22.2.en: Christ's going out and arriving at Golgotha took place during the third hour, that is, from the third hour to the sixth hour (see the commentary on ch. 20:2-7).

27.22.3.en: If people reject you, remember what they did to your Lord Jesus Christ, and endure for His sake as He endured for yours.

27.23.0.en: It was the custom of the Romans to give the one presented for crucifixion vinegar mixed with gall to drink, so that the one who drinks it would be partially numbed and bear the pains more easily. Some Jews used to offer vinegar mixed with gall as an act of mercy to one condemned to death, so it may be that some Jews were the ones who offered this vinegar to Christ. But Christ, who bore the bitterness of our sins, did not want to drink any anesthetic, so that He might bear all the toils of our sins, for He was: “wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon Him; and with His stripes we are healed” (Isa 53:5).

27.23.1.en: Mark the Evangelist mentions that they: “gave Him to drink wine mingled with myrrh” (Mk 15:23), and there is no disagreement with Matthew, who mentioned that it was vinegar, because the Roman soldiers used a cheap, sour kind of wine, whose taste resembles vinegar, and which, when mixed with myrrh, gives the same effect as wine in numbing the one who drinks it. It should be noted that the offering of wine mixed with bitterness to Christ before He was hung on the Cross is different from the second time, when they offered Him vinegar while He was hanging (v. 48), and when He said: “I thirst” (Jn 19:28).

27.24.0.en: The garments of Christ that clung to His body signify the Church, and the soldiers who crucified Him divided them into four parts among themselves, a symbol of His salvation offered to the four corners of the world. The Gentile soldiers took them, for His salvation is offered to the whole world: to Jews, Gentiles and everyone who believes in Him.

27.24.1.en: As for His coat, it was woven as one piece, and they cast lots for it. It signifies the one Church woven from above, that is, from heaven, and He wants it to live in one love without division.

27.24.2.en: The prophet David prophesied about Him (Ps 22:18) that His garments would be divided and lots cast for them. Crucifixion was a severe torture for the one crucified: after they stripped him, they nailed him by his hands and feet and left him hanging until he died, suffering from bleeding and harsh pains.

27.24.3.en: Crucifixion also meant shame and disgrace among the Romans, who ruled the world at that time.

27.24.4.en: The dividing of the garments shows how cruel people are, and how absorbed in acquiring material things while they torment others. Christ dies for our salvation, while we are busy dividing His garments or casting lots for them.

27.24.5.en: They used to lay the one to be crucified on the cross horizontally and nail him, then raise the cross and set it in a hole prepared for it, and fix it so that the feet of the crucified were raised from the ground about 30-40 cm.

27.24.6.en: Christ was nailed to the Cross at the end of the third hour; therefore Mark the Evangelist mentions that they crucified Him at the third hour (Mk 15:25), while John the Evangelist (Jn 19:14, 15) mentions that the end of Christ's trial by Pilate was about the sixth hour, that is, shortly before the end of the third hour. This was the period during which the going out from Jerusalem to Golgotha and the nailing of Christ to the Cross took place, so that by the sixth hour He had been hung on the Cross and the Cross fixed in the ground, and then there was darkness over all the earth (v. 45).

27.25.0.en: The Roman soldiers sat down to guard Jesus, though He is the Guardian of the whole world, but He humbled Himself and submitted in order to redeem us. Thus the guards become witnesses to His crucifixion and death, so that this would be proof of the power of His resurrection after death, and likewise no other man resembling Him was crucified, for He is the Christ whom Judas betrayed and the Jews tried, and who was crucified and died for the salvation of those who believe in Him.

27.26.0.en: The Romans wrote above the Cross that He was the King of the Jews, which was not what the priests and elders of the people wanted, but this was by divine permission, because He is the King of kings who redeems His people.

27.26.1.en: It was the custom to write the charge or the reason for the crucifixion, and what was meant was that the reason for Christ's crucifixion was His claim to be the King of the Jews, which was resistance to Caesar.

27.26.2.en: It is noted that the four Evangelists agreed that the reason for Christ's crucifixion was His claim to be the King of the Jews, and they recorded it as follows, bearing in mind that translation from different languages may bring some differences in expression:

27.26.3.en: Matthew: “This is Jesus the King of the Jews” (Mt 27:37).

27.26.5.en: Luke: “This is the King of the Jews” (Lk 23:38).

27.26.6.en: John: “Jesus of Nazareth the King of the Jews ...” (Jn 19:19).

27.26.7.en: It is noted that the two Evangelists Luke and John (Jn 19:20) added that what was written was in three languages, Hebrew, Greek and Latin.

27.27.0.en: Christ condescended to be among the wicked, for two thieves were crucified with Him, one on the right and one on the left, so that He might seek their salvation. The thief on the right believed in Him, and He received him in His paradise (Lk 23:40-43). Humble yourself among the weak and the despised in order to encourage them and draw them to Christ, so that they find their rest, as Christ humbled Himself and was crucified among the wicked.

27.28.0.en: Satan was in a state of constant doubt and uncertainty about the person of the Lord Jesus. And when he feared that the One hanging on the Cross might be the awaited Messiah, he tried to stop the work of redemption, and consequently the work of his own binding by Christ, by causing those who passed by Him to mock Him and provoke Him to come down from the Cross. They reminded Him of His words about His ability to destroy the Temple and build it in three days; that is, if He was able to do that as He claimed, and if He was also the Son of God as He says, let Him come down from the Cross. Yet He had not said this about Solomon's Temple, but about the temple of His body, which, when they crucify Him and He dies, He would raise up Himself on the third day. And this was the false testimony against Him, namely His saying that He would destroy the Temple of the Jews, which did not happen.

27.28.1.en: In this mockery there took part the Jews who passed by this place, as well as the chief priests (v. 41), and also the Roman soldiers (Lk 23:36). The provocations of Christ were many, so that He would come down from the Cross and not complete the work of redemption.

27.29.0.en: The chief priests also, with the scribes and elders, took part in mocking Him, saying that if He had worked miracles and healed the sick and raised the dead, let Him save Himself now. That is, they affirmed His helplessness and provoked Him to answer their slanders, attributing His former miracles to sorcery and a connection with the prince of demons, as proven by His inability now to save Himself, and mocking His claim to be the King of Israel, because their thinking about kingship is earthly, tied to power and material greatness, and not heavenly.

27.30.0.en: They continued their mockery of Christ, and said to Him: If You are the Son of God, and trusted in Him as You claimed, why did God not save You from torment and death? Your crucifixion confirms that You are not the awaited Messiah. This mockery was prophesied by David in detail in (Ps 22:7, 8).

27.31.0.en: Here another mockery and reproach comes to Him from one of the two thieves, the thief on the left (according to Church tradition), who said to Him: “If Thou be Christ, save Thyself and us” (Lk 23:39). It is written that the two thieves were reproaching Him, since the reproach of one of them indicates both, though the thief on the right did not take part in this evil reproach, as Luke the Evangelist mentions (Lk 23:40, 41), and the Holy Bible mentions that one of the two thieves believed in Him.

27.31.1.en: Therefore the Church has called him the thief on the right, since the right represents blessing and strength, while the left signifies distance from God.

27.31.2.en: Do not answer the wicked if they provoke you, so that you do not sin as they do, but flee with your life from anger, and so you will be truly strong like Christ and accomplish your goals.

27.32.0.en: Nature declared its mourning and its denunciation of what people were doing to their crucified God, for there was darkness over all the earth at midday while the sun was in its strength, from the sixth hour to the ninth according to Jewish reckoning, which is from twelve until three in the afternoon.

27.32.1.en: This darkness signifies the darkness of sin in which the world lived, which Christ was crucified to lift from us. It was also a declaration of nature's grief over the crucifixion and death of its Creator, and a warning to the wicked so that they would repent, as the thief on the right repented and believed.

27.33.0.en: “About the ninth hour”: that is, near the end of the sixth hour.

27.33.1.en: “Eli”: a Hebrew word meaning: my God, and in Syriac: Eloi or Eloi, as Mark the Evangelist mentioned (Mk 15:34). “My God ... my God, why hast Thou forsaken me?”: a well-known and memorized Jewish expression, for it is the first verse of Psalm 22, which points to clear prophecies about the sufferings and crucifixion of Christ. In it David prophesied about: (1) The contempt and mockery of the people (vv. 6-8).

27.33.3.en: (3) The piercing of His hands and feet (v. 16).

27.33.4.en: (4) The dividing of His garments and the casting of lots for them (v. 18).

27.33.5.en: For this reason Christ used it, as though saying to the Jews: Go back to what David wrote about Me, so that you may know what you are doing to Me.

27.33.6.en: It is not meant, of course, that God forsook Him, because He is God incarnate, and the Son and the Father are one essence. Christ's cry announces the severity of the sufferings He endures, whether bodily or spiritual, because He bears the sins of the whole world, and He is the Holy God who is repelled by sin, and so He reveals its hideousness.

27.34.0.en: The Jews who stood by and heard Him thought that He was calling Elijah, because the word Eli resembles Elijah, and also because they believe that Elijah will come a second time. So they mocked Him, saying: Look, will Elijah come to save Him? This is a rhetorical question of denial, meaning that Elijah will not come.

27.34.1.en: And Christ declared His thirst and said: I thirst (Jn 19:28), to confirm His humanity, for the crucified feels intense thirst. So one came forward and offered Him vinegar to drink, and put it in a sponge and put it on a reed of hyssop, as John the Evangelist mentions (Jn 19:29). Hyssop is a plant whose branches were used for sprinkling holy water according to Jewish rites.

27.35.0.en: By this Christ completed all the sufferings on our behalf, so He cried with a loud voice to express the intensity of the pain, and died on the Cross, and His spirit departed, separated from His body, and thus redemption was accomplished; but His divinity remained united to His body and also to His spirit.

27.35.1.en: Christ spoke seven sayings while on the Cross, which are:

27.35.2.en: (1) His prayer for those who were crucifying Him, saying: “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Lk 23:34).

27.35.3.en: (2) His promise of Paradise to the repentant thief, saying: “Today shalt thou be with Me in paradise” (Lk 23:43). (3) His entrusting the Virgin, His mother, to John, saying to her: “Woman, behold thy son,” then saying to John: “Behold thy mother” (Jn 19:26, 27).

27.35.4.en: (4) His cry to God from the intensity of the pain, saying: “Eli ... Eli, lama sabachthani” (Mt 27:46). (5) His saying: “I thirst” (Jn 19:28).

27.35.6.en: (7) The giving up of His spirit to God, saying: “Father, into Thy hands I commend My spirit” (Lk 23:46).

27.35.7.en: Look at the sufferings of Christ on the Cross so that you feel His love for you, and so love Him at all times.

27.36.s.en: (9) Events accompanying the death of Christ

27.36.0.en: At the death of Christ at the ninth hour, the veil of the Temple was rent. It was a huge curtain of cloth, about 7 meters wide and 14 meters high, separating the Holy Place from the Holy of Holies (+1). Only the priests could see this rending, for they alone were permitted to enter the Holy Place, and some of them believed and announced what had happened.

27.36.1.en: The rending of the veil is a second sign of the end of the Jewish priesthood and the beginning of the Christian priesthood (the first sign was in ch. 26:56, when Caiaphas the high priest tore his clothes). For Christ accomplished redemption on the Cross as High Priest, offering Himself as a sacrifice for us, and by His death He opened for us the way into the Holy of Holies, that is, the paradise of bliss and the Kingdom of Heaven. In the Old Testament no one was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies except the high priest, with blood to sprinkle on the Ark of the Covenant. But now Christ the High Priest, by the rending of His body, that is, His death on the Cross, has opened for us the way into the Holy of Holies, so that we can not only look at the sanctuary and the altar in the Church, but partake of His most holy Body and Blood.

27.36.2.en: “The earth did quake, and the rocks rent”: this means the shaking of nature before the divine salvation accomplished on the Cross. In the spiritual, symbolic sense, it signifies the shaking of earthly lusts, which Christ has lifted from us, and the breaking open of stony hearts so that He may dwell in them.

27.37.0.en: In addition to the Temple and nature being affected, death too was affected, and it no longer had authority over the children of God, for the graves were opened, and many bodies of the saints who slept (the believers) arose. By His Cross He had transferred them from Hades to Paradise, and by their resurrection they declare their joy in the salvation they received. They came out of the graves after His resurrection, and went into the holy city, that is, Jerusalem, because the Temple of God was in it, and appeared to many to proclaim the resurrection and salvation to the Jews so that they would believe in Christ the Redeemer, whether they were well-known saints such as the prophets and men of God, or Jews who believed in the awaited Messiah and had died a short time before and were known to the people in Jerusalem.

27.37.1.en: (+) To bring this closer to the reader's mind, the Temple consisted of three main parts: the outer court, which corresponds to the nave of the church today, where the people could be present; and the two inner parts (the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies), which no one was permitted to approach except the priests. They can be likened to the sanctuary and the altar in our churches.

27.38.0.en: When the centurion and the soldiers with him, who were responsible for guarding the crucified Christ (and who were Roman Gentiles), saw the changes in nature, the earthquake and the splitting of the rocks, in addition to their having witnessed the earlier darkness, they declared that Christ was not an ordinary man, but they feared Him as God, and said: “Truly this was the Son of God,” believing His word about Himself that He was the Son of God, as they had learned from the crowds who passed by the Cross.

27.38.1.en: John the Evangelist mentions (Jn 19:31) that at this time the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken so that they would die and their bodies not remain hanging on the feast of Passover and Unleavened Bread, which lasts eight days. He agreed, and the soldiers broke the legs of the two thieves, and when they came to Christ they found that He was already dead, so one of the soldiers pierced His side with a spear to make sure of His death, and blood and water came out.

27.39.0.en: There was a group of women who used to follow and minister to Christ with their means, and who had come with Him from Galilee, in the north of Judea, to Jerusalem. Among them were Mary Magdalene, out of whom He had cast seven demons, Mary the wife of Clopas or Alphaeus, the sister of the Virgin Mary, and Salome, the mother of James and John the sons of Zebedee. They were watching from afar, either out of fear of the Jews, or because the soldiers had kept them away, but their love made them follow everything to the end.

27.39.1.en: God shows you signs in the events of life so that you believe in Him and trust in Him. You can understand them if you hold fast to your relationship with Him in prayers, fasts, readings and partaking of the Holy Sacraments. And if you understand what is happening around you, do not neglect it, but let it be a motive for you to repent and to increase your relationship with God.

27.40.0.en: One of the disciples of Christ, that is, His followers, was called Joseph of Arimathea, Arimathea being near Jerusalem. He was one of the elders of the Jews, of the council of the seventy elders, and he was rich, and he had not agreed with the opinion of the Jewish elders concerning the crucifixion of Christ (Lk 23:51).

27.40.1.en: By virtue of his connections and position, he was able, with boldness and faith, to go in to Pilate and ask for the body of Jesus after He had died, and Pilate permitted him. By this act he exposed himself to danger from Pilate and the Jews, because it was evidence of his strong attachment to the crucified Christ, but he did not fear, and God preserved him so that no one harmed him.

27.41.0.en: Joined with Joseph of Arimathea was Nicodemus, who believed in Christ but secretly, like Joseph, for fear of the Jews, and he brought spices and aloes, which the two placed on the body (Jn 19:39). Then Joseph took the body and wrapped it in clean linen.

27.41.1.en: Linen is used for the rich, since He is the King of kings, and it is also the garment of the priests, since He is our High Priest who offered Himself as a sacrifice on the Cross.

27.42.0.en: Joseph owned a garden near the place of the Skull, in which was a rock in which he had hewn a tomb for himself. When Christ died, he preferred Him to himself and laid Him in his new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. This was by God's providence, to confirm His resurrection, so that there would be no other bodies or bones with Him that might be suspected of having risen. And he rolled a great stone to the door of the tomb which no one could easily roll away, to confirm that the disciples of Christ could not steal the body without a noise that the guards of the tomb would notice.

27.43.0.en: Some women, in their love for Christ, were still watching His burial. The Holy Bible mentions among them Mary Magdalene and the other Mary, whom Mark the Evangelist mentions to be the mother of Joses (Mk 15:47), and Luke mentions that: “the women also, which came with Him from Galilee, followed after, and beheld the sepulchre, and how His body was laid. And they returned, and prepared spices and ointments; and rested the sabbath day according to the commandment” (Lk 23:55, 56), and John mentions: “Now there stood by the cross of Jesus His mother, and His mother's sister, Mary the wife of Cleophas” (Jn 19:25). Your love for God makes you watch His ways and walk behind Him, not only in times of ease but also in afflictions, holding fast to His commandments. So be bold and declare your love for Him however much the wicked reject the way of God.

27.44.0.en: “The chief priests and Pharisees”: the members of the council of the Sanhedrin.

27.44.1.en: “That deceiver”: they still called Christ by that name, despite their having seen the darkness and the earthquake, because they were insistent on evil.

27.44.2.en: On the evening of Friday, that is, the beginning of the Sabbath, since the day begins from its night, and after the end of Friday, which the Jews call the Preparation for the Sabbath, after the burial of Christ, the chief priests and Pharisees remembered the words of Christ about His resurrection when He: “said unto them, Destroy this temple [that is, His body], and in three days I will raise it up” (Jn 2:19). They may have learned from one of His disciples His prophecy about His rising on the third day (ch. 16:21), and they feared that the disciples would steal His body and claim that He had risen. So they went to Pilate and told him of this, and asked him to order the securing of the tomb, that is, the placing of seals and guards upon it, and they did not understand that by this they would confirm His resurrection when He rises on the third day despite the presence of seals and guards. “The last error”: since they considered all Christ's teaching an error that misled the people, then if the disciples stole His body and claimed that He had risen, they would mislead the people more than during the days of Christ's life among them.

27.45.0.en: Pilate permitted them to secure the tomb, so they went and made the tomb secure with Roman guards and seals; and of course they did everything with precision to make sure the body would not be stolen. Do not be troubled by the schemes of the wicked and their power, for God turns them to your benefit and to the revealing of your righteousness. The resurrection of Christ His appearing to His disciples
